title: Transcatheter Directed Interventions in Pulmonary Embolism: Recent Evidence, Guidelines and Challenges.
journal: Journal of cardiovascular development and disease
abstract: Acute pulmonary embolism (PE) is a major cause of cardiovascular mortality, and managing patients at risk of deterioration despite anticoagulation is challenging. Transcatheter interventions, including catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) and mechanical thrombectomy (MT), aim to rapidly unload the right ventricle while limiting the bleeding risk of systemic thrombolysis. Their use long preceded robust evidence, but recent randomised trials have changed this. In normotensive patients with right ventricular dysfunction and elevated cardiac biomarkers, low-dose CDT, with or without ultrasound, reduced early clinical deterioration in two trials with differing eligibility criteria: HI-PEITHO required troponin elevation and at least two additional markers of cardiorespiratory compromise, whereas PRAGUE-26 required troponin or natriuretic peptide elevation. No statistically significant difference in major bleeding was detected, although mortality did not improve and intracranial haemorrhage occurred. MT accelerated right ventricular recovery versus anticoagulation and, in an open-label trial against CDT, improved a composite driven by deterioration and intensive care use. Guidelines predate most of these data and differ between continents: the 2019 European Society of Cardiology guideline and European consensus documents reserve transcatheter treatment mainly for high-risk PE with contraindicated or failed thrombolysis and for rescue after deterioration, whereas the 2026 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline allows its consideration in incipient cardiopulmonary failure. This review summarises techniques, evidence and recommendations, and it discusses patient selection, comparative effectiveness and long-term outcomes. Pending updates, decisions should be individualised by multidisciplinary PE response teams.

title: Interventional reperfusion for pulmonary embolism.
journal: JAAPA : official journal of the American Academy of Physician Assistants
abstract: The management of patients with intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism (PE) has evolved in recognition of this unique population's potential for circulatory collapse. Systemic thrombolysis, catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT), and mechanical thrombectomy are reperfusion therapies typically reserved for patients with high-risk PE. Intermediate-risk PE represents a dynamic pathophysiologic state, whereby right ventricular dysfunction (RVD) may progress to cardiogenic shock in minutes to hours. More recent evidence suggests that early reperfusion for patients with intermediate-risk PE can have a profound impact on mortality (and adverse bleeding events) compared with anticoagulation alone. Anticoagulation is paramount in PE management, although recent trends highlight a reliance on unfractionated heparin despite evidence favoring alternative anticoagulation strategies. Modern perspectives on PE management emphasize early identification of RVD and escalation to interventional reperfusion, using vasoactive medications as a bridge to therapy.

title: How to identify patients with low-risk acute pulmonary embolism: clinical implications and knowledge gaps.
abstract: Acute pulmonary embolism (APE) is a common disease, affecting 75-269 out of 100,000 people each year. The clinical spectrum of APE is broad, ranging from asymptomatic or mild dyspnea to shock and cardiac arrest. A significant number of patients could be treated on an outpatient basis; however, there are no clear criteria for selecting individuals who could be safely treated at home. Although there is evidence of the safety and effectiveness of selection for home treatment based on the simplified Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (sPESI) or the Hestia criteria, further analyses showed the benefits of combining these criteria with assessment of right ventricular dysfunction (RVD) on imaging and laboratory biomarker testing (troponins and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide [NT-proBNP]). Another issue that should not be neglected is the assessment of bleeding risk associated with anticoagulant treatment initiation. This state-of-the-art review provides a comprehensive overview of risk stratification in patients with APE, focusing particularly on low-risk patients who can be safely treated at home.

title: Temporary Mechanical Circulatory Support in Pulmonary Embolism.
abstract: This article highlights the limitations of thrombolysis in high-risk pulmonary embolism and the emerging role of temporary mechanical circulatory support, especially venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, as a bridge to recovery or definitive therapy. The pathophysiology of right ventricular failure in pulmonary embolism, risk stratification strategies, and decision-making frameworks for initiating mechanical circulatory support are reviewed. Further, we cover practical considerations, including device selection, circuit management during thrombectomy, and the imperative for preanesthesia planning in risk mitigation. Finally, this article highlights the importance of conducting prospective and randomized studies on device choice, timing, and integration with reperfusion strategies.

title: Intensive Care Unit Management of the Hemodynamically Significant Pulmonary Embolism.
abstract: Acute pulmonary embolism remains a major cause of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, with prognosis determined by right ventricular (RV) adaptation to the abrupt rise in pulmonary vascular resistance. Although most cases can be managed outside the intensive care unit, patients with RV failure, hemodynamic instability, or cardiac arrest require advanced monitoring and intervention. Management in this setting emphasizes rapid diagnosis and risk stratification, timely initiation of reperfusion therapies, and carefully tailored hemodynamic and respiratory support. Optimal outcomes rely on multidisciplinary collaboration, early escalation of care, and individualized, evidence-based decision-making.

title: Advances in Risk Stratification of Pulmonary Embolism.
abstract: Normotensive patients with pulmonary embolism (PE) experience highly variable outcomes. Despite advances in clinical prediction tools, echocardiography, and computed tomographic imaging, there is no universally agreed upon strategy to identify which normotensive patients with PE are at risk of decompensation. This article reviews the current state of evidence and recent advances in risk prediction tools, echocardiography, and imaging to predict clinical deterioration.

title: Pathophysiology of Right Ventricular Failure in Pulmonary Embolism.
abstract: Acute pulmonary embolism (PE) is a potentially life-threatening condition that can precipitate obstructive shock, a form of circulatory failure caused by the mechanical obstruction of blood flow through the pulmonary circulation. This article explores the pathophysiological mechanisms linking massive PE to obstructive shock, highlighting key diagnostic challenges, and the importance of rapid recognition in the emergency setting. We examine current strategies for risk stratification, imaging, and laboratory testing, as well as emerging biomarkers that may aid in early identification. The article also evaluates the efficacy and limitations of therapeutic interventions, including systemic thrombolysis, catheter-directed therapies, and surgical embolectomy, in the context of hemodynamic instability. Understanding the complex interplay between PE and obstructive shock is essential for optimizing outcomes in critically ill patients.

title: Two Faces of the Same Thrombus: Molecular Phenotypes of Thromboinflammation in Acute Pulmonary Embolism and the Path to Phenotype-Guided Risk Stratification.
abstract: Acute pulmonary embolism (PE) is a potentially fatal cardiovascular emergency where early risk assessment determines treatment escalation. Clinical scores like PESI and sPESI are useful but capture only a single moment and cannot track evolving biological processes: coagulation on inflamed endothelium, nitric oxide signaling loss, and right ventricular pressure overload. Circulating biomarkers provide direct readouts of these events. This review proposes that acute PE molecular pathophysiology organizes into two overlapping phenotypes-two faces of the same thrombus. The first is a predominantly thromboinflammatory phenotype, driven by neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), complement activation, and endothelial injury; the second is a predominantly myocardial phenotype, driven by right ventricular pressure overload and subendocardial ischemia. We examine each phenotype's molecular basis and appraise how far corresponding biomarkers-D-dimer, cardiac troponins, natriuretic peptides, GDF-15, H-FABP, sST2, complement activation products, and inflammatory indices-have moved into clinical practice. Two issues deserve attention: biomarker kinetics during the first 72 h after symptom onset, and whether intermediate-risk patients can be separated into meaningful molecular phenotypes. We address implementation barriers: lack of harmonized assays, undefined decision thresholds, and absence of prospective multicenter validation. This narrative review connects disease mechanisms to which patients are most likely to deteriorate and outlines a research agenda for phenotype-guided risk stratification.
